lead: Silicon is only useful once you can put dopants in chosen places. Three unit processes do that work. Oxidation grows a silicon dioxide layer that insulates, masks and protects. Diffusion moves dopant atoms into the crystal using heat alone. Ion implantation fires dopants in with a set energy and a set dose, so the depth is chosen in keV rather than guessed from a furnace schedule. Every CMOS flow uses all three: the gate oxide, the wells and the shallow source-drain extensions all come from this chapter's steps.
prereq: You need: donors, acceptors, carrier concentration and the MOS structure from Unit 1; the mask window itself is opened in 2.2.

blocks.text: Silicon oxidises easily, and the oxide it forms is a dense, stable insulator that sticks to the silicon beneath it. That is why silicon won: one material supplies both the semiconductor and its own insulator. SiO<sub>2</sub> does three jobs on a chip — gate insulator, field insulator between devices, and a mask that dopants cannot pass through.

Thermal oxidation grows this layer in a furnace at 900–1100 °C. Dry oxidation uses oxygen: Si + O<sub>2</sub> → SiO<sub>2</sub>. Wet oxidation uses steam: Si + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → SiO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>. Wet growth is many times faster, so it makes thick field oxide. Dry growth is slow and gives a denser film with fewer defects, so it makes the thin gate oxide, where a few nanometres decide the threshold voltage (see Unit 1, Threshold voltage and body effect).

blocks.where: x_ox is the oxide thickness in μm; t is the oxidation time in hours; A (μm) and B (μm²/h) depend on temperature and on whether the gas is O<sub>2</sub> or H<sub>2</sub>O; τ is a small time offset covering oxide already present.

items: Thin oxide, reaction-limited: x_ox ≈ (B/A)(t + τ). The surface reaction is the bottleneck, so growth is linear in time.
Thick oxide, diffusion-limited: x_ox ≈ √(B·t). The oxidant must now diffuse through oxide already grown, so growth slows to a square root.
Growing 1 μm of oxide consumes about 0.44 μm of silicon, so the oxide surface sits above the original wafer surface.
Field oxide is thick and wet-grown; gate oxide is thin and dry-grown, often only 2–10 nm.

blocks.text: A dopant atom inside silicon hops from lattice site to site at random, but a concentration gradient makes the hops carry more atoms downhill than uphill. Fick's first law states the flux: J = −D(∂C/∂x). J is the flux in atoms cm⁻² s⁻¹, D the diffusion coefficient in cm²/s, C the concentration in cm⁻³ and x the depth; the minus sign says flow goes from high concentration to low.
Conservation of atoms gives Fick's second law, ∂C/∂t = D(∂²C/∂x²).

blocks.where: D is the diffusion coefficient in cm²/s; D<sub>0</sub> is a material constant; E<sub>a</sub> is the activation energy, about 3–4 eV for common dopants in silicon; k = 8.62×10⁻⁵ eV/K is Boltzmann's constant; T is the absolute temperature in kelvin. Near 1000 °C, D roughly doubles for every 30 °C rise, so furnace temperature sets junction depth.

blocks.text: A doping step has two parts. Predeposition holds the wafer at a lower temperature in a gas carrying the dopant; the surface concentration saturates at the solid solubility and a fixed dose enters. Drive-in switches the gas off and raises the temperature; dopants spread deeper and the surface concentration falls. Most of the dose ends up within one diffusion length of the surface, L = 2√(Dt), with L in cm, D in cm²/s and t in s.

blocks.where: C is the concentration in cm⁻³ at depth x and time t; Q is the dose in cm⁻²; D is the diffusion coefficient; t is the time. At x = L = 2√(Dt) the concentration has fallen to 1/e of its surface value.

blocks.text: Diffusion is isotropic: dopant spreads sideways under a mask edge by the same distance it spreads down. Layout must reserve room for that lateral spread; the design rules in 2.6 encode it.

sections.h3: Ion implantation: placing dopants by energy

blocks.text: Diffusion cannot make a doping that is shallow, heavy and precisely placed. Ion implantation can. Dopant atoms are ionised, accelerated through 30–200 keV and fired at the wafer. They enter the crystal, lose energy by nuclear collisions and by electronic drag, and stop at a depth set by the energy.

Two numbers describe the step. The dose φ is the number of ions per unit area, in cm⁻², typically 10¹¹ to 10¹⁶ cm⁻². The energy is in keV; more energy means a deeper stop. The average stopping depth is the projected range R<sub>p</sub>, and the spread around it is the straggle ΔR<sub>p</sub>.

blocks.where: C(x) is the implanted concentration in cm⁻³ at depth x; φ is the dose in cm⁻²; R<sub>p</sub> is the projected range in cm; ΔR<sub>p</sub> is the straggle in cm. The peak value, at x = R<sub>p</sub>, is about 0.4φ/ΔR<sub>p</sub>.

blocks.text: If the beam lines up with a crystal channel, ions slip between rows of atoms and travel far deeper, leaving a long tail. The fix is to tilt the wafer about 7° from the beam and rotate it, so no channel is open. Masking works the other way: an ion stops inside resist or oxide when R<sub>p</sub> is less than the mask thickness. The same oxide window that defines a pattern therefore defines the doping, so the implant is self-aligned and needs no extra mask.

The collisions knock silicon atoms off their sites, leaving a damaged, partly amorphous layer. A short anneal at 900–1000 °C repairs the lattice and moves dopants onto substitutional sites, which activates them. Anneal too long or too hot and the profile you placed diffuses away. That balance is the process engineer's daily trade.

examples.question: At 1000 °C the diffusion coefficient of phosphorus in silicon is D = 3×10⁻¹⁴ cm²/s. A drive-in lasts t = 1 hour. (a) Find the diffusion length L = 2√(Dt). (b) Is the resulting junction shallower or deeper than 0.5 μm? (c) How long would a diffusion length of 0.5 μm take?
steps: Convert the time to the units D is given in: t = 1 hour = 3600 s.
Form the product: D·t = 3×10⁻¹⁴ cm²/s × 3600 s = 1.08×10⁻¹⁰ cm².
Take the square root: √(D·t) = √(1.08×10⁻¹⁰) cm = 1.04×10⁻⁵ cm.
Multiply by 2: L = 2 × 1.04×10⁻⁵ cm = 2.08×10⁻⁵ cm = 0.21 μm.
Compare with 0.5 μm: 0.21 μm is smaller, so the junction is shallower.
For L = 0.5 μm = 0.5×10⁻⁴ cm, first halve it: √(D·t) = 0.25×10⁻⁴ cm.
Divide by D: t = 6.25×10⁻¹⁰ / 3×10⁻¹⁴ s = 2.08×10⁴ s.
Convert to hours: t = 2.08×10⁴ / 3600 h = 5.8 hours.
examples.answer: L = 0.21 μm after one hour, which is shallower than 0.5 μm; reaching 0.5 μm would take about 5.8 hours.

import math
D = 3e-14
t = 3600.0
L = 2*math.sqrt(D*t)
print(round(L*1e4, 2))
target = 0.5e-4
t2 = (target/2)**2 / D
print(round(t2/3600, 1))

traps: Dose is per area (cm⁻²); concentration is per volume (cm⁻³). A 10¹⁵ cm⁻² implant spread over 0.1 μm gives about 10²⁰ cm⁻³, not 10¹⁵ cm⁻³.
Diffusion is isotropic and implantation is directional. Only the implant keeps a junction shallow without sideways spread, which is why source-drain extensions use it.
Wet oxide is fast and thick, dry oxide is slow and dense. Gate oxide is dry, field oxide is wet — not the other way round.
Deal-Grove: linear for thin oxide (reaction-limited), parabolic for thick (diffusion-limited). Examiners deliberately swap the two labels.
The anneal that repairs implant damage also diffuses the profile. It must be the minimum that activates the dopants — usually seconds at 900–1000 °C, not an hour.

quiz.q: Name the two oxidising ambients used in thermal oxidation and the reaction each gives.
quiz.a: Dry: oxygen, Si + O₂ → SiO₂. Wet: steam, Si + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 2H₂.

quiz.q: Why does oxide growth slow down as the film gets thicker?
quiz.a: The oxidant must reach the silicon by diffusing through the oxide already grown. In the thick-film limit that diffusion, not the surface reaction, limits the rate, so x_ox grows as √(B·t) instead of linearly.

quiz.q: Give typical temperature and energy ranges for oxidation/diffusion and for implantation, and say why they differ so much.
quiz.a: Oxidation and diffusion run at 900–1100 °C because they rely on thermally activated atomic motion. Implantation is a physical ballistic process, so it runs at room temperature with energies of 30–200 keV; only the anneal afterwards needs heat.

quiz.q: An implant has dose φ = 10¹⁵ cm⁻², R_p = 0.10 μm and ΔR_p = 0.03 μm. Find the peak concentration.
Dry oxidation at 1000 °C has B/A = 0.107 μm/h. Using the linear limit, how long does 0.03 μm of gate oxide take?
quiz.a: x = (B/A)·t, so t = 0.03/0.107 h = 0.28 h = about 17 minutes.

quiz.q: A 0.5 μm field oxide is wanted but the furnace gives only 0.2 μm. Assuming the parabolic regime, how much longer must the oxidation run?
quiz.a: In the parabolic regime x ∝ √t, so t ∝ x². The factor is (0.5/0.2)² = 6.25, so the run must be 6.25 times longer.

quiz.q: Why is the wafer tilted about 7° during implantation?
quiz.a: To prevent channeling. If the beam is parallel to a major crystal direction, ions travel between atom rows and stop far deeper than R_p, leaving an unwanted tail; the tilt plus a rotation closes every channel.

quiz.q: What is the difference between predeposition and drive-in?
quiz.a: Predeposition keeps a dopant source on the surface at a lower temperature, so a fixed dose enters at the solubility limit. Drive-in removes the source and raises the temperature, so the existing dopants spread deeper and the surface concentration drops.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern fabs run these steps for seconds, not hours: rapid thermal oxidation, spike anneals and millisecond laser anneals exist because an hour at 1000 °C moves a 20 nm junction far too much. Thermal SiO₂ has been partly replaced as the gate insulator by plasma-nitrided oxide and by high-k dielectrics such as HfO₂, because a 1 nm oxide leaks by tunnelling. Implants now use molecular clusters and cryogenic wafer temperatures to keep damage shallow and activation high. To go further, search for rapid thermal processing, high-k metal gate, plasma doping and cryogenic implantation.
